items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1960-01-03
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] That's right. That's Larry Shields, who, of course... Harry Shields, rather. The clarinet player. And we have a recording of it now by the original Dixieland jazz band...

ctx.x: That's right. That's Larry Shields, who, of course... Harry Shields, rather. The clarinet player. And we have a recording of it now by the original Dixieland jazz band at the jazz band ball. 楽 The End The End The End The End Fine. And that was at the jazz band Ball. Now to get back to our interview with world famous Nick LaRocca, the daddy of jazz. Nick, for the next record we have selected, which will be coming up in a moment or two, we have Delivery Stable Blues. Now, that's a very interesting name. Was there a…

Well, there was a story connected with it. There was a litigation. One of the men in the early Chicago bands that I had let go, he wanted a piece of it, which I thought he wasn't entitled to, because the tunes were mine.

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-05-26
items.q: until we had Harry Shields to come up. Who was the brother? Larry Shields.

ctx.x: And he had some very nice things to say about you and talked about your playing. So you'll be happy to know that other people are backing your story up. If you go to the musicians, some of them will. And Raymond is one of them who will back you up.

Well, Sharky might because Sharky got up and Sharky lost his place in the jazz club by telling the people I was the one who brought this music around the world. Sharky was pulled off a program for the same thing. Now, Sharky was born about eight, nine years old when I was a musician playing music. Sharky wasn't playing music. Harry Shields wasn't playing music. Parenti wasn't playing music. George's Brunessons that they played. They weren't around. But they all got their mouth open big as an alligator trying to…
Now, I know you or I, we don't want to take credit away from Bix for what he had. Bix is a great man. Yes.
